name: The Allegory of the Cave
plain_explanation: Prisoners chained in a cave since childhood see only shadows cast on a wall and mistake them for reality; a prisoner who escapes into the sunlight discovers the real world for the first time, and if he is a true philosopher he will feel bound to return and try to enlighten those still chained, even though they will think him a fool.
precise_definition: Plato's extended simile (Republic Book VII) in which prisoners bound in an underground den, seeing only firelit shadows on a wall, represent ordinary humanity confined to sense-perception and opinion; escape into sunlight represents the philosopher's ascent, through dialectic, to knowledge of the Ideas and ultimately of the Good.
why_it_mattered: It is, per Russell, 'perhaps the most influential' part of the Republic, conveying Plato's epistemology and political vision (the philosopher's duty to rule, however unwelcome, over those still trapped in opinion) in a single vivid image.
historical_origin: Built on the earlier analogy of sight requiring light, with the sun standing for the Idea of the Good.
examples: 'Human beings living in an underground den... they see only their own shadows, or the shadows of one another, which the fire throws on the opposite wall of the cave.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: A recurring image in later philosophy and theology for the ascent from ignorance to enlightenment.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The returning philosopher's duty to the prisoners parallels the guardian's duty to rule; Russell notes a Christian Platonist might read it as prefiguring the Incarnation.
